prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose and poetry in which memory, the body and dream are built into a vast metaphysical architecture.

statement.case_for: My first-place view of Cărtărescu rests on the common criteria, not on agreement among colleagues. The case is distinctiveness of voice, formal and linguistic ambition, and imaginative depth. From public knowledge, the Orbitor trilogy (Blinding is its first volume) and Solenoid turn memory, the body and dream into a large, patterned metaphysical structure. The poetry and early fiction suggest a unified project, not a single peak. The work also connects to what I value in literature that lets past and present, the living and the dead, be intertwined. I note that as context, not as evidence of preference. A single-writer citation is clean, because the project is coherent, the credit is unambiguous and the language is Romanian throughout. After reading my colleagues' openings I still find the case persuasive. The reservations raised about the late work concern how to weigh scale and recursion, and they do not undermine the core achievement.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that my judgment rests on translations of very long, dense prose. The effect of Romanian syntax and rhythm, which may be central to the achievement, cannot be confirmed here. Corpus coverage is also uneven: the poetry and early work are thinner in my knowledge than the major novels. Some colleagues suggest that the encyclopedic, recursive scale may in places become over-extended or repetitive, and I cannot dismiss this without a full reading. The risk is that a citation built on the large novels would credit the oeuvre more evenly than my evidence supports.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for the scale, patterning and unmistakable voice. She also flags that the late work may be repetitive or over-extended in places, and that the poetry and early work are less known.
responses.response: I accept the qualification and share the uncertainty. I cannot rule out stretches of repetition in the later novels, and I would not claim otherwise. The question for the citation is whether recurrence is the method or a weakness. In a project built on recursive memory and bodily imagery, repetition seems to belong to the form, but I hold that as a hypothesis and not a finding. I would therefore keep the citation anchored in the sustained project and not in any one late volume. I would also want the committee to read what exists of the poetry before we credit it.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg praises the construction of an inner cosmological world from personal and bodily experience. He notes that the excess and encyclopedic density could be weighed differently across the committee. He ranks Adonis second and gives weight to timing because of the poet's age.
responses.response: I agree that density is where the committee may reasonably differ, and I would not defend excess as a virtue in itself. My view is that the density is disciplined by recurring structures and images, so it is not simply accumulation. On Adonis, I ranked him lower in my opening, mainly because my access to the Arabic prosody and intertextual force is the weakest of any candidate on the list. Your argument about his formal renewal of the language is serious and has moved me to keep him as an alternative. I do not accept age or timing as a literary argument for him, and I think you would agree that the case has to stand on the work.

responses.point: Sward ranks Cărtărescu first for visionary voice and a place within the European novel tradition. She also leaves open whether the later novels sustain the originality of the earlier ones. She places Alexis Wright third and Adonis second.
responses.response: The open question about the later novels is the right one, and it is the point where my confidence is lowest. I would put it this way: Solenoid reads in public discussion as an intensification of the earlier project, not as a retreat, but that rests on reception and not on my own reading. On Wright, I rank her fourth and share your regard for the formal reinvention of the novel through oral and ecological time. My hesitation is the compact fiction corpus, two major novels, which makes sustained quality over a career harder to judge than for Cărtărescu. I would not let the political significance of her work carry the argument, and your opening is careful about this too.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Zurita second, arguing that his poetry gives collective memory and loss a monumental form with a clear formal and moral center. He also notes that the landscape-scale works are harder to weigh as literature.
responses.response: I ranked Zurita seventh, and I want to be precise about why. It is not a doubt about the intensity or the voice. The weight I cannot settle is the share of the achievement that lies in the sky-writing and desert inscriptions and not in the printed sequences, together with how much of his incantatory rhythm survives translation. If the committee can establish that the printed poems carry the achievement alone, I would revise my ranking upward. Until then, I would not use the historical context of dictatorship to fill that gap, because subject alone does not establish merit.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first and notes that the poetry and early work are less well covered in the supplied entry. She ranks Anne Carson third and raises whether hybrid and visual works fit the will's phrase 'literary works'.
responses.response: I agree that the poetry coverage is a gap in the evidence. I would not let the citation claim more than what the committee has actually assessed. On Carson, whom I ranked second, your question about hybrid and visual works is also mine, because Nox depends on its form as an object. I think the stronger case is on the verse novel and the original writing, and I am less sure that the scholarly and translational work belongs in a literary citation. That uncertainty is why I keep her as an alternative and not as my preferred candidate.

uncertainties: Whether Romanian syntax, rhythm and the density of the long novels carry in translation, so that my judgment of linguistic achievement is not overstated.
Whether the later novels sustain or merely repeat the originality of the earlier work, which I cannot settle without a full reading.
How much of the poetry and early work exists in translation, and whether it supports a citation that names poetry as well as prose.
How to weigh Adonis fairly given the limits of translation for Arabic prosody and intertextuality, since my own access to that corpus is indirect.
Whether the extra-textual and object-based works of Zurita and Carson belong to the literary core. I have not independently verified any source or read the full corpus of any candidate.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My work on Selma Lagerlöf and my own fiction are context and not evidence of favor for any shortlisted writer, and my ties to committee colleagues are ordinary professional ones.
